sub: Named after naṣr, “help”, in ayah 1; also called “the Farewell”
theme: When Allah’s help comes, Makkah is conquered, and people enter Islam in crowds, the Prophet’s ﷺ mission is complete. The response is not celebration but glorifying Allah, praising Him and asking His forgiveness.
story: Madinan, and the last complete surah to be revealed. One report says it came at Minā during the Farewell Pilgrimage, shortly before the Prophet ﷺ passed away; others place it earlier, before or around the conquest of Makkah.

The Prophet ﷺ understood it as news that his life was nearing its end. When ʿUmar asked the senior veterans of Badr about it, some said it commands praise and forgiveness at victory. A young Companion said it announced the Prophet’s ﷺ death, and ʿUmar agreed.
Afterwards the Prophet ﷺ often said in his bowing and prostration: “Glory be to You, O Allah, our Lord, and praise be to You. O Allah, forgive me.” He strove for the Hereafter harder than ever.

sections.title: When Allah’s help and victory come
sections.meaning: When Allah’s help and the conquest of Makkah arrive, and you see people entering Allah’s religion in crowds, then glorify your Lord with praise and ask His forgiveness. He always accepts repentance.
points: Allah’s help and the conquest arrive
People enter Allah’s religion in crowds
Glorify, praise and seek forgiveness; He accepts repentance
sections.matters: It shows how to meet success: with humility, praise and seeking forgiveness, not pride. It also told the Prophet ﷺ that his mission was complete and his time was near, since great deeds are sealed with seeking forgiveness.
sections.story: Arab tribes had been waiting to see whether the Prophet ﷺ would overcome his own people. Once Makkah was conquered, they came in whole delegations to accept Islam, and within two years Arabia had embraced it.
explained: Naṣr Allāh is Allah’s help for His Prophet ﷺ against his enemies, and al-fatḥ is the conquest of Makkah. Before it, people entered Islam one or two at a time. After it, they came afwājā: in crowds, whole tribes at once, many becoming its helpers after being its enemies.

The command is not to celebrate but fa-sabbiḥ bi-ḥamdi rabbik: declare Allah free of every fault while praising Him, and wa-staghfirh: ask His forgiveness. Innahu kāna tawwābā: He keeps accepting repentance. The Prophet ﷺ read it as a sign that his task was done and his time was near.
teaches: Credit every success to Allah, not to yourself.
Meet blessings and victories with more praise and seeking forgiveness.
Seal good deeds by asking Allah’s forgiveness.
Increase your worship as you get closer to meeting Allah.
sections.hook: Ayah 1 names two gifts (naṣr, fatḥ); ayah 3 gives two commands (sabbiḥ, istaghfir). Ayah 2 is the scene in between: people entering in crowds (afwājā).

groups.text: When Allah’s help and the conquest of Makkah come, people enter Allah’s religion in crowds.
Then glorify your Lord with praise and ask His forgiveness; He always accepts repentance.

1.explain: Naṣr Allāh: Allah’s help for His Prophet ﷺ against his enemies. Al-fatḥ: the conquest of Makkah. Idhā, “when”, frames it as a sign to watch for.
1.why: Reports differ on timing: at Minā during the Farewell Pilgrimage, shortly before the Prophet ﷺ passed away, or earlier, around the conquest of Makkah. It was the last complete surah revealed.

2.explain: Afwājā: in crowds, whole tribes at once. The tribes had waited to see if he would overcome Quraysh; after the conquest they came in delegations, many from Yemen.

3.explain: Sabbiḥ bi-ḥamdi rabbik: glorify your Lord while praising Him. Istaghfirh: ask His forgiveness. Tawwāb: He accepts repentance again and again. The Prophet ﷺ took it as a sign his life was ending.
